items.stem: An 82-year-old client with several chronic conditions is starting a new oral medication. According to safe prescribing principles for older adults, which nursing action best reduces medication-related risk?

options.text: Encourage starting at the highest labelled adult dose to achieve a rapid effect.
Advocate for starting at the lowest effective dose and using the fewest medications necessary.
Advise crushing all extended-release tablets to improve absorption.
Recommend adding two over-the-counter supplements without reviewing the current regimen.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Older adults are more susceptible to adverse effects; starting at the highest adult dose increases toxicity risk.
rationales.B: Correct. Merck advises starting medications at the lowest effective dose and using the fewest medications necessary; OpenStax urges the least complicated regimen and review for drugs that can be discontinued.
rationales.C: Incorrect. OpenStax notes some capsules and extended-release pills should remain intact.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Adding supplements without reconciliation increases polypharmacy and interaction risk.

sources.title: 1.4 Special Considerations

items.stem: An ambulatory older adult who has fallen twice in the past year takes several medications, including an opioid analgesic. Which intervention should the nurse prioritize to reduce future fall risk related to medications?

options.text: Advise that fall-risk medications cannot be changed once prescribed.
Collaborate for a medication review to stop or minimize fall-risk drugs when possible and use the lowest effective dose.
Increase the opioid dose at bedtime so the client sleeps through the night and avoids toileting.
Discourage medication review because falls are inevitable with aging.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Merck states medications that increase fall risk should be stopped when possible or adjusted to the lowest effective dose.
rationales.B: Correct. Merck recommends reviewing medications for fall-risk impact and stopping or dose-adjusting when possible; OpenStax notes narcotics increase fall risk in older adults and require caution and teaching.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Increasing an opioid can worsen sedation and fall risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Fall risk can be reduced with multifactorial interventions including medication review.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching a family how to communicate with an older adult who has age-related hearing loss (presbycusis). Which actions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Face the client so the speaker’s mouth is visible.
Reduce competing background noise when possible.
Encourage use of prescribed hearing aids or assistive listening devices.
Speak only from another room so the client practices listening.
Shout directly into one ear from behind the client.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck notes lip-/speech-reading helps discrimination and that professionals should position so the listener can see the speaker’s mouth.
rationales.B: Correct. OpenStax identifies noise as a physical communication barrier and advises reducing extraneous noise; Merck describes modifying noisy listening environments.
rationales.C: Correct. OpenStax recommends hearing aids or assistive listening devices for age-related hearing loss.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Speaking from another room removes visual speech cues and worsens understanding.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Shouting from behind prevents lip-reading and can distort speech.

items.stem: An older adult living alone reports nearly falling at home after tripping on a throw rug in a dim hallway. For each nursing recommendation, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated to reduce environmental fall risk.

rows.text: Clear walkways of clutter and secure or remove loose throw rugs.
Improve lighting in hallways and pathways used at night.
Encourage rushing to the bathroom in the dark to minimize time out of bed.
Keep frequently used paths free of furniture that blocks movement.
Add more loose scatter rugs for softer flooring in every room.

rationales.R1: Indicated. OpenStax advises clearing pathways and notes rugs increase fall risk; Merck identifies environmental hazards as extrinsic fall factors.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Inadequate lighting, especially at night, is a situational/environmental fall risk addressed by improving lighting.
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Merck lists rushing to the bathroom at night with inadequate lighting as a situational fall risk.
rationales.R4: Indicated. Clearing furniture that obstructs pathways reduces environmental hazards.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Additional loose rugs increase trip hazards rather than reduce them.

items.stem: An Ontario RN is deciding whether aspects of care may be performed by an unregulated care provider (UCP). Which client situation best supports assigning or having a UCP perform the activity?

options.text: The client’s condition is unstable and expected to change unpredictably over the shift.
The client has established, well-defined care needs, a well-controlled condition not expected to change, and the UCP’s competence for the activity has been verified.
The RN has never verified the UCP’s competence but the procedure looks straightforward.
The activity requires nursing evaluation of an evolving response to a new medication titration.

rationales.A: Incorrect. CNO’s decision tree asks whether the client’s condition is well controlled/managed and not expected to change; OpenStax likewise requires stable condition with expected outcomes before delegating.
rationales.B: Correct. CNO lists established well-defined needs and a well-controlled condition not expected to change among client factors, and requires knowing the UCP is competent for the client in the given circumstances; OpenStax right circumstance requires stability with expected outcomes.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CNO states a nurse cannot assume UCP competence regardless of how straightforward a procedure appears.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Evaluating response to treatment requires nursing judgment and is not appropriate UCP work in this context.

items.stem: While preparing an intravenous antibiotic, a nurse notices the wrong vial was nearly selected and stops before administration. What is the most appropriate next action in a culture of safety?

options.text: Discard the near miss quietly without reporting because no harm occurred.
Report the near miss through the organization’s safety reporting process so system improvements can be made.
Administer a double dose of the correct antibiotic to compensate for the almost-error.
Blame a coworker publicly at the nursing station without documenting the event.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Near misses are learning opportunities; failing to report prevents system improvement.
rationales.B: Correct. OpenStax describes reporting near-miss incidents so practice and policy can improve; AHRQ defines a culture of safety as including a blame-free environment where individuals can report errors or near misses without fear of reprimand.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Administering an unauthorized double dose is unsafe and unrelated to near-miss learning.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A just/safety culture emphasizes nonpunitive reporting and system learning, not public blaming.

items.stem: A public health nurse helps organize a community program that offers fecal immunochemical testing (FIT) to asymptomatic adults to detect colorectal cancer early. Which level of prevention does this activity represent?

options.text: Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Quaternary prevention

rationales.A: Incorrect. Primary prevention aims to prevent disease occurrence (for example, immunization campaigns), not detect existing subclinical disease.
rationales.B: Correct. OpenStax defines secondary prevention as early disease detection in healthy-appearing individuals with subclinical disease; CDC explains colorectal screening finds polyps/cancer early when treatment works best.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Tertiary prevention targets clinical disease to reduce severity and sequelae after diagnosis.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Quaternary prevention is not the OpenStax framework level described for population screening programs in this context.

sources.title: 15.2 Health Promotion and Disease Prevention Interventions
sources.evidence: Secondary prevention emphasizes early disease detection in healthy-appearing individuals with subclinical forms of disease.

sources.title: Screening for Colorectal Cancer
sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.evidence: Screening can find polyps before they turn into cancer and find colorectal cancer early, when treatment works best.

items.stem: A community health nurse teaches a household preparedness class. Which teaching point best reflects recommended personal disaster preparedness?

options.text: Wait until a disaster is announced before gathering any water or food supplies.
Assemble a household emergency kit in advance with multi-day water and non-perishable food, and know where the kit is kept.
Rely solely on neighbours to provide all medications after an emergency begins.
Store the only household kit in a locked attic that no family member can access quickly.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Preparedness includes accumulating supplies before a disaster occurs.
rationales.B: Correct. OpenStax states preparedness plans include accumulating disaster supplies; Ready.gov recommends a multi-day water/food kit kept in a designated, ready-to-grab location.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Ready.gov advises organizing prescription medications as part of the kit because pharmacies may be inaccessible.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The kit should be ready and known to household members for quick use or evacuation.

items.stem: A parent asks what fever medicine is safe for a 7-year-old with influenza-like illness. Which teaching is correct?

options.text: Give aspirin (ASA) because it is the preferred antipyretic for influenza.
Avoid aspirin (ASA); use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed because aspirin increases Reye syndrome risk with certain viral illnesses.
Any salicylate-containing product is required to prevent Reye syndrome.
Aspirin is safer than acetaminophen for chickenpox and influenza in school-age children.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Merck and CPS advise avoiding aspirin in children because of Reye syndrome risk with illnesses such as influenza and varicella.
rationales.B: Correct. Merck states aspirin should be avoided in children because it increases Reye syndrome risk with influenza and varicella; CPS Caring for Kids likewise warns not to use ASA for fever when chickenpox, influenza, or certain other viral infections are present.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Salicylates increase, rather than prevent, Reye syndrome risk in this setting.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Aspirin is specifically discouraged for chickenpox and influenza in children.

items.stem: A toddler presents to the emergency department with a barky cough and mild croup without stridor at rest. Which pharmacologic intervention is most consistent with evidence-based croup management?

options.text: Withhold all corticosteroids because mild croup never benefits from steroids.
Administer a single dose of dexamethasone as directed, which is recommended across mild to severe croup presentations.
Start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics as first-line therapy for typical viral croup.
Give repeated high-dose aspirin for airway inflammation.

rationales.A: Incorrect. CPS recommends considering corticosteroids for all children presenting with croup from mild to severe; Merck also uses a long-acting glucocorticoid such as dexamethasone for mild disease.
rationales.B: Correct. CPS states dexamethasone (commonly 0.6 mg/kg orally once) is highly efficacious and steroids are the cornerstone across severity; Merck lists a single dose of long-acting glucocorticoid (e.g., dexamethasone) for mild croup.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Typical croup is viral; antibiotics are not first-line for uncomplicated viral croup.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Aspirin is not croup therapy and is unsafe in children with viral illness because of Reye syndrome risk.

sources.title: Acute management of croup in the emergency department
sources.evidence: Corticosteroids should be considered for all children with croup from mild to severe; oral dexamethasone is highly efficacious.

sources.title: Croup
sources.evidence: For mild disease, cool humidified air and often a single dose of a long-acting glucocorticoid (eg, dexamethasone).

items.stem: A school-age client with cystic fibrosis and pancreatic insufficiency is preparing to eat lunch. Which medication teaching is correct?

options.text: Skip pancreatic enzyme capsules on days when stools look normal.
Take pancreatic enzyme replacement with meals and snacks as prescribed.
Take pancreatic enzymes only at bedtime, never with food.
Stop enzymes permanently once antibiotic therapy for a pulmonary exacerbation begins.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Enzyme replacement is ongoing therapy for pancreatic insufficiency, not based on a single stool observation.
rationales.B: Correct. Merck states pancreatic enzyme replacement should be given with all meals and snacks in pancreatic insufficiency; OpenStax identifies administering pancreatic enzymes as a key gastrointestinal nursing intervention for CF.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Enzymes are timed with food to aid digestion/absorption, not reserved for bedtime only.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Antibiotics treat infection; they do not replace the need for enzyme therapy for pancreatic insufficiency.

items.stem: An older adult is admitted after a fall with a suspected lower-extremity fracture. Which assessment finding set should the nurse prioritize when monitoring the injured limb?

options.text: Only wound drainage colour, ignoring pulses and sensation.
Neurovascular checks including pain, pulse, pallor, paresthesia, and paralysis (the 5 Ps).
Skin turgor on the contralateral arm as the sole priority assessment.
Capillary blood glucose every hour instead of limb perfusion checks.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Fracture nursing care requires neurovascular monitoring for perfusion and nerve function, not drainage colour alone.
rationales.B: Correct. OpenStax directs frequent neurovascular examinations using the 5 Ps; Merck likewise emphasizes assessing for neurovascular injury and compartment syndrome signs (pain, pallor, paresthesias, coolness, pulselessness).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Contralateral skin turgor does not assess distal perfusion of the injured extremity.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Glucose monitoring does not replace neurovascular assessment of a fractured limb.

sources.title: 13.3 Bone Fractures
sources.section: Nursing Care of the Patient with Bone Fractures
sources.evidence: Perform frequent neurovascular examinations for the 5 P’s: pain, pulse, pallor, paresthesia, and paralysis.

sources.title: Overview of Fractures
sources.evidence: Assess for neurovascular injury and compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, pallor, paresthesias, coolness, pulselessness).
